title: Best RAM for Ryzen 7 9800X3D (2026): 5 DDR5 Kits Ranked
description: 32 GB of DDR5-6000 CL30 is the best RAM for a Ryzen 7 9800X3D, and the G.Skill Flare X5 is our pick: EXPO, 1:1 UCLK, 1.35 V, 33 mm tall. 5 kits ranked.
dek: The 9800X3D needs less from its memory than any other Ryzen 9000 chip. Buy two 16 GB sticks of DDR5-6000 CL30, turn on EXPO, and spend the rest on the GPU.
intro: The G.Skill Flare X5 32GB (2x16GB) DDR5-6000 CL30 is the best RAM for the Ryzen 7 9800X3D. It runs the AM5 sweet spot of DDR5-6000 at CL30, which keeps the memory controller at a 1:1 ratio with the memory clock, and it does so at a rated 1.35 V in a 33 mm tall stick that fits under any air cooler.

This guide is for anyone pairing memory with a 9800X3D, whether in a new build or a drop-in upgrade on an existing AM5 board. The chip is DDR5 only, so every pick is a DDR5 kit with an AMD EXPO profile. DRAM prices have swung hard since late 2025, so every price here is a wide USD band.
quickAnswer: Buy the G.Skill Flare X5 32GB DDR5-6000 CL30 ($110–$200) for a 9800X3D gaming PC. The Corsair Vengeance and Kingston Fury Beast DDR5-6000 CL30 kits are equal alternatives in the same band, so buy whichever is cheapest. The TeamGroup T-Force Delta RGB ($120–$210) adds lighting, and the 64 GB G.Skill Trident Z5 Neo RGB ($220–$400) suits streaming and creative work.

picks.label: Best Overall
picks.bestFor: most 9800X3D gaming builds, especially under a large dual-tower air cooler
picks.skipIf: you want RGB lighting or need more than 32 GB
writeup: The Flare X5 is the kit to buy for a Ryzen 7 9800X3D. It runs DDR5-6000 at CL30 with timings of 30-38-38-96, which works out to a 10 ns first-word latency. More important on AM5, DDR5-6000 is the speed that almost every Ryzen 7000 and 9000 chip can run with the memory controller clock (UCLK) at a 1:1 ratio with the memory clock (MCLK). That is the setting that avoids a latency penalty, and it is where AMD and most reviewers point 9800X3D owners.

G.Skill built it around AMD EXPO, so one BIOS setting takes you from the default JEDEC speed to the rated one. It is rated at 1.35 V, a little lower than the 1.40 V that most rival DDR5-6000 CL30 kits need.

Height is the other reason it wins. At about 33 mm, the Flare X5 slides under the front fan of the Thermalright Phantom Spirit 120 SE and Peerless Assassin 120 SE, the coolers most 9800X3D builders buy, without moving the fan up. There is no RGB, which keeps the price down.
The catch is price volatility. Like every DDR5 kit, the Flare X5 has swung between about $110 and $200 since late 2025. Check the Corsair and Kingston equivalents on the day.
pros: About 33 mm tall, clears any air cooler
cons: Price has swung widely since late 2025

picks.label: Runner-Up
picks.bestFor: 9800X3D builders who want a widely stocked, well-known brand at the sweet-spot speed
picks.skipIf: you cannot confirm the listing is the EXPO version
writeup: Corsair's Vengeance 32GB DDR5-6000 CL30 is a near twin of the Flare X5 for a 9800X3D. Same capacity, same two-stick layout, same DDR5-6000 speed and CL30 latency. Its timings are listed as 30-36-36-76, slightly tighter on paper in the secondary numbers, but independent memory scaling reviews show kits at this speed and CAS latency land very close together in games, and on an X3D chip the gap is smaller still.

Pay attention to the version. Corsair sells this kit in an Intel XMP 3.0 version and an AMD EXPO version under similar names. For a 9800X3D, buy the EXPO one. XMP kits often boot at their rated speed on AM5 boards too, but the EXPO profile is written with AMD's memory controller in mind, so it is the lower-risk choice and the one board makers list on their support pages.
It is rated at 1.40 V and stands about 35 mm tall, a couple of millimeters taller than the Flare X5. That still fits under the front fan of the common dual-tower coolers.
It sits second only because the Flare X5 has the lower voltage and height. If the Corsair is cheaper when you order, buy it. Its band is the same $110–$200.
cons: Easy to buy the XMP version by mistake
1.40 V vs 1.35 V on the Flare X5

picks.label: Best Backup Kit
picks.bestFor: 9800X3D builders who buy whichever sweet-spot kit is cheapest that week
picks.skipIf: you want lighting from the same listing
writeup: The Kingston Fury Beast 32GB DDR5-6000 CL30 completes the trio of plain kits that suit a 9800X3D equally well. It has the same speed and CAS latency as the two kits above, an AMD EXPO profile, a 1.40 V rating and a heat spreader about 34.9 mm tall. On a 9800X3D there is no game where you would notice a difference between these three.

That is the point of listing it. With DDR5 prices moving week to week since late 2025, the best kit is often the one on sale. When the Flare X5 and Vengeance both sit near the top of the $110–$200 band and the Fury Beast is $20 lower, buy the Kingston and put the savings toward the graphics card, which sets your frame rate far more than any memory change will.
Kingston backs the kit with a limited lifetime warranty, and Fury Beast part numbers appear on many motherboard qualified vendor lists.
Kingston also sells an RGB version of the Fury Beast. It is a separate listing with a taller heat spreader, so check height before you pick it under a big air cooler.
pros: Same speed and latency as the top picks
cons: Nothing beyond price sets it apart
RGB version is a separate, taller kit

picks.label: Best 64 GB Kit
picks.bestFor: 9800X3D owners who also stream, edit video, run VMs or play heavily modded games
picks.skipIf: you only game, where 32 GB is enough at about half the price
writeup: The G.Skill Trident Z5 Neo RGB 64GB (2x32GB) DDR5-6000 CL30 is the kit to buy when 32 GB runs short. It keeps the same DDR5-6000 CL30 speed, so the memory controller stays at 1:1, and it carries an EXPO profile rated at 1.40 V. The Neo line is G.Skill's AMD-focused Trident Z5 range.

The 9800X3D is a gaming chip first, so who needs 64 GB? Mostly owners who do more at the same time. Streaming with OBS while a game and browser run, editing high-resolution video, keeping virtual machines open, or loading large simulation and strategy mod lists can all push past 32 GB. For gaming alone, the extra capacity will mostly sit idle.

Buy 64 GB as two 32 GB sticks, never as two 2x16 GB kits. Four DDR5 sticks put twice the load on AM5's memory controller, and boards often cannot hold DDR5-6000 with all four slots filled. The 32 GB sticks in this kit are dual-rank, which is a little harder to train than single-rank 16 GB sticks, but a two-stick dual-rank kit at DDR5-6000 is a common AM5 setup.
It costs $220–$400, roughly double a 32 GB kit, and stands about 44 mm tall. If heavy all-core work is the reason for 64 GB, the Ryzen 9 9950X3D may suit you better than the 9800X3D.
cons: Roughly double the price of 32 GB

picks.label: Best RGB Kit
picks.bestFor: showcase 9800X3D builds with a glass side panel and an AIO or single-tower cooler
picks.skipIf: you run a large dual-tower air cooler whose front fan sits over the DIMM slots
writeup: If you want lit memory in a 9800X3D build, the TeamGroup T-Force Delta RGB 32GB DDR5-6000 CL30 is the sensible way to get it. It runs the same DDR5-6000 CL30 sweet spot as the plain kits, so you give up nothing in speed, and its wide ARGB light bar is one of the more striking designs at this price.

Buy the EXPO version. TeamGroup sells the Delta RGB with XMP or EXPO profiles depending on the version, and like the Corsair, the EXPO one is the right match for an AM5 board. The lighting is usually controlled through your motherboard's RGB software, so there is no extra app to install.

Height is the trade-off. At about 46 mm, the Delta RGB is roughly 13 mm taller than the Flare X5. The front fan on a dual-tower cooler like the Phantom Spirit 120 SE sits over the first DIMM slot, so a kit this tall may force you to raise the fan, which adds to the cooler's total height. A single tower such as the Arctic Freezer 36 or a 240 mm or 360 mm AIO avoids the problem entirely.
It usually runs $10 to $20 more than the plain kits, in a $120–$210 band since late 2025. That is a fair premium for lighting, provided it fits.
cons: Can clash with dual-tower air coolers

ranking.intro: We ranked these kits for the Ryzen 7 9800X3D using AMD's published memory specifications and EXPO guidance, memory makers' spec sheets, motherboard qualified vendor lists, published independent memory scaling reviews, owner reports from AM5 builders and recent US street prices. None of these kits were bench-tested by us. The ER Score is a research score. Because DRAM prices have swung hard since late 2025, we rank on platform fit first and treat price as a band.
criteria: DDR5-6000, the fastest speed nearly every Ryzen 9000 chip runs with UCLK equal to MCLK.
CL30 at DDR5-6000, a 10 ns first-word latency.
An AMD EXPO profile so rated speed takes one BIOS setting.
Two sticks only. 32 GB for gaming, 64 GB in two 32 GB sticks for heavier use.
Height under the dual-tower coolers most 9800X3D owners use, and rated voltage.
Recent US street-price ranges, with the late-2025 DRAM price jump in mind.
ranking.why: The Flare X5 won because it pairs DDR5-6000 CL30 and EXPO with the lowest rated voltage and the lowest height of the five kits.

mentions.name: DDR5-6400 CL32 kits
mentions.text: DDR5-6400 CL32 has the same 10 ns first-word latency as DDR5-6000 CL30 with slightly more bandwidth. Many Ryzen 9000 chips can hold 1:1 at that speed, but not all, so you may need to drop the memory controller ratio or the speed. On a 9800X3D the possible gain is too small to justify the risk.

mentions.name: 48 GB (2x24 GB) DDR5 kits
mentions.text: Kits built from 24 GB sticks give 48 GB while keeping each stick single-rank, which is easy on AM5's memory controller. They are a reasonable middle ground for a 9800X3D owner who streams, but they are less common than 2x16 GB and 2x32 GB kits, so check speed and latency carefully before buying.

mentions.name: DDR5-8000 and faster kits
mentions.text: Very fast kits force AM5's memory controller to half rate, and they usually need a strong memory controller, a two-slot board and manual tuning to run reliably. With the 9800X3D's 96 MB of L3 cache cutting trips to RAM, the money is far better spent on the graphics card.

sections.h: What RAM Speed Is Best for the Ryzen 7 9800X3D?
body: DDR5-6000 CL30 is the best speed for the Ryzen 7 9800X3D. AMD's official rating for the chip is DDR5-5600, but that is the speed AMD guarantees on every CPU and board without any profile enabled. With EXPO turned on, DDR5-6000 is the widely recommended sweet spot for Ryzen 7000 and 9000, because nearly every chip can run it with the memory controller in sync with the memory. AMD has also pointed to DDR5-6000 as the sweet spot for AM5.

CL30 is the tightest CAS latency kits commonly reach at that speed without a big price premium. To compare kits, convert CAS latency to nanoseconds: multiply CL by 2,000 and divide by the speed in MT/s. Lower is better. Secondary timings and bandwidth also matter, so treat it as a guide.

sections.h: What Is the 1:1 UCLK:MCLK Ratio, and Why Does It Matter?
body: Ryzen 9000 chips have three clocks that matter for memory. MCLK is the memory clock, half the DDR5 data rate, so DDR5-6000 means an MCLK of 3,000 MHz. UCLK is the clock of the memory controller inside the CPU. FCLK is the Infinity Fabric clock that links the CPU's chiplets.

At 1:1, UCLK runs at the same 3,000 MHz as MCLK, and data passes between the memory and the controller without waiting. Push the memory much past DDR5-6000 and most chips can no longer hold that, so the board drops UCLK to half the memory clock, a 1:2 ratio. The added latency from that switch usually cancels the extra bandwidth of the faster kit, at least in games. That is why DDR5-6000 CL30 often matches or beats far more expensive kits on AM5.

Unlike AM4, where DDR4-3600 lined up the Infinity Fabric with the memory, AM5 runs FCLK separately. Most boards set it to around 2,000 MHz automatically, and you do not need to touch it. When EXPO loads a DDR5-6000 profile, most current AM5 BIOS versions also set UCLK to 1:1 on their own.
Our [AMD EXPO](/glossary/amd-expo/) and [Infinity Fabric](/glossary/infinity-fabric/) glossary entries explain the terms in more depth.

sections.h: Why Does 3D V-Cache Narrow the Gains From Faster RAM?
body: The 9800X3D carries 96 MB of L3 cache, three times the 32 MB on the Ryzen 7 9700X. AMD gets there by bonding an extra 64 MB cache die to the compute die. Games repeatedly touch the same chunks of data, and with that much cache, far more of it stays on the chip instead of making the slower trip out to system memory.

Every trip to RAM that the cache avoids is a trip where memory speed and latency do not matter. So while faster memory still helps a 9800X3D a little, the effect is smaller than on standard Ryzen chips. Independent reviews widely report that X3D parts gain less from memory tuning than chips like the 9700X, and the same pattern held on the earlier 7800X3D, which also has 96 MB of L3.

This changes how you should spend. On a 9800X3D, moving from a slow DDR5-4800 default to DDR5-6000 CL30 with EXPO is still worth doing, because it costs nothing once you own the kit. Paying a large premium beyond that rarely shows up in games, especially at 1440p and 4K, where the graphics card sets the pace. Our [best GPU for Ryzen 7 9800X3D](/best-gpu-for-ryzen-7-9800x3d/) guide is the better place to put the money.
If you are still choosing between X3D chips, see [9800X3D vs 7800X3D](/compare/ryzen-7-9800x3d-vs-ryzen-7-7800x3d/). Both use the same DDR5 kits and the same advice applies.

Buy 2x16 GB for a gaming build and 2x32 GB if you also stream, edit or run virtual machines. 32 GB covers current games with Discord, a browser and launchers open in the background, and 16 GB sticks are single-rank, the easiest load for AM5's memory controller.

The 32 GB sticks in a 2x32 GB kit are usually dual-rank. That makes them slightly harder to train and can mean slightly different secondary timings, but a two-stick dual-rank kit at DDR5-6000 is a well-trodden AM5 setup and the right way to reach 64 GB. If your work is heavily multi-threaded rather than gaming, the 16-core Ryzen 9 9950X3D may be the better chip; see [9800X3D vs 9950X3D](/compare/ryzen-7-9800x3d-vs-ryzen-9-9950x3d/).

Do not plan to add a second 2x16 GB kit later. Four DDR5 sticks on AM5 often will not run at EXPO speed, AMD's official supported speed drops sharply with four modules, and two separate kits may use different memory chips even under the same part number.

sections.h: How Do You Turn On EXPO for a 9800X3D?
body: Every kit here boots at a slow default JEDEC speed, often DDR5-4800, until you enable its EXPO profile. Many new builders never do, which leaves performance on the table. It takes a minute, and you should update the BIOS first.
list: Update the motherboard BIOS. Older B650 and X670 boards need a Ryzen 9000-ready BIOS to boot a 9800X3D at all, and later versions improved DDR5 compatibility.
Enter the BIOS, usually with Delete or F2 at boot.
Find the memory profile setting. Board makers label it EXPO, AMD EXPO or a combined EXPO/XMP option.
Select the first EXPO profile, DDR5-6000 CL30 for every kit on this page, then save and exit.
Wait through the first boot. AM5 boards train the memory and can sit on a black screen for a minute or more. Do not power off.
Turn on Memory Context Restore if your BIOS offers it, so later boots skip full retraining.
Check the speed in Windows Task Manager under Memory. It should read 6000 MT/s.

sections.h: Will the RAM Fit Under Your 9800X3D Cooler?
body: Check memory height against your cooler before you buy. Most 9800X3D builders use a dual-tower air cooler, and on those the front fan usually sits over the first DIMM slot. Low kits around 33 to 35 mm fit with the fan in its normal position. Taller RGB kits around 44 to 46 mm may need the fan raised, which adds a few millimeters to total height and can then clash with the case side panel.

Single-tower coolers and AIO liquid coolers leave the slots clear, so any kit fits. Our [best CPU cooler for Ryzen 7 9800X3D](/best-cpu-cooler-for-ryzen-7-9800x3d/) guide lists cooler heights and RAM overhang for each pick.

sections.h: Why Have DDR5 Prices Swung So Much?
body: DRAM prices have swung hard since late 2025, and they have stayed volatile through 2026. The main driver is demand from AI data centers. Memory makers have moved production toward high-bandwidth memory and server DRAM, leaving less capacity for the consumer DDR5 sticks that go into gaming PCs.

That is why the bands here are wide: $110–$200 for a plain 32 GB DDR5-6000 CL30 kit, $120–$210 for the RGB kit, and $220–$400 for 64 GB. The three plain 32 GB kits are interchangeable on a 9800X3D, so compare all three on the day, set price alerts, and do not pay extra for a brand or for lighting when the same speed and latency costs less elsewhere.
If prices spike while you are building, a DDR5-5600 or DDR5-6000 CL36 EXPO kit is a reasonable stopgap. The 9800X3D's large cache softens the cost of a looser kit.

sections.h: Which Motherboard Settings Matter for 9800X3D Memory?
body: Very few. Any AM5 board with a current BIOS runs DDR5-6000 EXPO kits on a 9800X3D. Two sticks belong in the slots the manual marks for two DIMMs, usually A2 and B2, the second and fourth slots from the CPU.

Our [best motherboard for Ryzen 7 9800X3D](/best-motherboard-for-ryzen-7-9800x3d/) guide covers which boards suit the chip. For memory, check for a BIOS flashback button and whether your kit is on the board's qualified vendor list.

mistakes: The 9800X3D is an AM5 chip, and AM5 is DDR5 only. DDR4 sticks have a different notch and will not fit the slots. If you are moving from an AM4 system, your old DDR4 kit cannot come with you, so budget for a new DDR5 kit.

A DDR5-6000 kit runs at its JEDEC default, often DDR5-4800, until you enable EXPO in the BIOS. That leaves a free gain unused. Turn on the profile, wait through the long first boot, and confirm 6000 MT/s in Task Manager.
Four DDR5 sticks on AM5 often will not hold EXPO speed and can take a long time to train. For 64 GB, buy a 2x32 GB kit like the Trident Z5 Neo rather than two 2x16 GB kits.
Paying for speed the 9800X3D cannot use
Kits beyond DDR5-6400 usually push the memory controller to half rate, and the 9800X3D's 96 MB of L3 already blunts memory gains. A pricey DDR5-8000 kit adds little in games over DDR5-6000 CL30.
Buying the XMP version by mistake

Corsair and TeamGroup sell the same kit in XMP and EXPO versions with similar names. XMP kits often work on AM5, but the EXPO version is made for AMD's controller. Check the part number before you check out.
bottomLine: For a Ryzen 7 9800X3D, buy 32 GB of DDR5-6000 CL30 in two sticks, enable EXPO and stop there. The G.Skill Flare X5 is our pick for its 1.35 V rating and 33 mm height, with the Corsair Vengeance and Kingston Fury Beast as equal alternatives when they cost less. Choose the T-Force Delta RGB for lighting and the 64 GB Trident Z5 Neo RGB for streaming or creative work. DRAM prices have swung hard since late 2025, so compare on the day.

faqs.q: What is the best RAM for the Ryzen 7 9800X3D?
faqs.a: The best RAM for the Ryzen 7 9800X3D is a 32 GB (2x16GB) DDR5-6000 CL30 kit with an AMD EXPO profile, such as the G.Skill Flare X5. That speed keeps the memory controller at 1:1 on AM5. DRAM prices have swung hard since late 2025, so expect $110–$200.

No. The 9800X3D uses socket AM5, which supports DDR5 only. DDR4 sticks will not physically fit AM5 motherboard slots. If you are upgrading from an AM4 system with DDR4, you need a new AM5 board and a new DDR5 kit.

faqs.q: What RAM speed does AMD rate the 9800X3D for?
faqs.a: AMD rates the Ryzen 7 9800X3D for DDR5-5600. That is the speed AMD guarantees without overclocking profiles. DDR5-6000 with EXPO is widely run on the chip and is the commonly recommended sweet spot, because it keeps the memory controller at a 1:1 ratio with the memory clock.

faqs.q: Does RAM speed matter for the 9800X3D?
faqs.a: RAM speed matters less on the 9800X3D than on standard Ryzen chips. Its 96 MB of L3 cache keeps more game data on the chip, so independent reviews show smaller gains from faster memory. DDR5-6000 CL30 with EXPO is still worth it, but costlier kits rarely pay off in games.

faqs.q: Is 32 GB of RAM enough for a 9800X3D?
faqs.a: Yes, 32 GB is enough for a 9800X3D gaming PC. It covers current games with background apps open. Choose 64 GB, as a 2x32 GB kit, only if you also stream, edit video, run virtual machines or play heavily modded games that use more memory.

faqs.q: Is DDR5-6400 better than DDR5-6000 for the 9800X3D?
faqs.a: Not in a way that justifies the risk. DDR5-6400 CL32 and DDR5-6000 CL30 share a 10 ns first-word latency. Some 9800X3D chips hold 1:1 at 6400 and some do not, and with the large L3 cache the bandwidth gain is small. DDR5-6000 CL30 is the safer buy.

faqs.q: Can I use four sticks of RAM with a 9800X3D?
faqs.a: You can, but it is not recommended. Four DDR5 sticks put more load on AM5's memory controller, so they often will not run at EXPO speed, and AMD's supported speed drops sharply with four modules. Buy two sticks: 2x16 GB for gaming or 2x32 GB for 64 GB.

faqs.q: Will XMP RAM work on a 9800X3D?
faqs.a: Often yes, but EXPO is the better match. Many AM5 boards can read XMP profiles and run them, sometimes with timing changes. An EXPO kit's profile is written for AMD's memory controller, so it is the lower-risk choice. Corsair and TeamGroup sell EXPO versions of the kits on this page.
